--- Page 1 ---
Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
Anran Liu, Benzhao Hou, Zongsheng Cao, Daichao Wang, Lang Chen, and Shitong Chen∗
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language
optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current
agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store
reusable experience at the instance level. We introduce Ar-
chOR, an archetype-centric skill agent that builds on Opt-
Skills by adding two retrieval-focused modules. Centroid-
Aware Representation Learning (CARL) refines the ordering
of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype
residual.
Signature-Guided Retrieval (S3R) attaches open-
dimensional structural signatures to skills, prioritizes can-
didates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic
re-ranking to a top-K set.
A baseline-preserving arbitra-
tion rule determines when the structural route should replace
the original selector.
Experiments on the same five opti-
mization benchmarks with the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
backbone and the unchanged released skill library show that
these access-level changes produce consistent improvements
in solver-verified accuracy.
1
Introduction
Operational optimization underlies many industrial decision
pipelines, including routing, production scheduling, energy
dispatch, and workforce planning. Turning these business
descriptions into executable models is still a labor-intensive
expert task: practitioners must identify decision variables,
formalize constraints, choose objectives, and translate the
formulation into solvercode. Large language models(LLMs)
have therefore become an attractive interface for optimization
modeling. Recent systems improve this interface through
multi-agent orchestration (AhmadiTeshnizi, Gao, and Udell
2024; Xiao et al. 2024), domain-oriented fine-tuning (Jiang
et al. 2025a; Huang et al. 2025a), or reinforcement learning
with solver feedback (Chen et al. 2025; Ding et al. 2026).
However, strong benchmark accuracy does not by itself
solve the reuse problem that matters in practice.
A de-
ployed modeling agent should recognize that two differ-
ently narrated requests may instantiate the same optimiza-
tion archetype, route repeated instances through a stable
workflow, and extend its library when the distribution shifts.
Recent experience-based systems move in this direction: Al-
phaOPT (Kong et al. 2025) maintains solver-verified insights,
∗Corresponding author: Shenzhen University.
while LEAN-LLM-OPT (Liang et al. 2026) retrieves struc-
tured exemplars to seed workflow construction. Their stored
artifacts are still largely instance-centered, so surface narra-
tives, noisy descriptions, and missing coverage can distort
retrieval even when the underlying mathematical structure is
familiar.
The central difficulty is that optimization skills are defined
by structure rather than by wording alone. Two assignment
problems can mention different commodities, agents, and
budgets while requiring the same variable pattern and con-
straint family; conversely, two descriptions can share terms
such as “distribute” or “mix” while calling for incompatible
formulations. A raw cached vector and a natural-language
skill card have no explicit reason to preserve these archetype
boundaries, leaving robust generalization and in-distribution
routing unresolved. A convincing skill-reuse system should
therefore show that its retrieval space and selection rules
align with optimization structure.
We address this issue with ArchOR, an archetype-centric
skill agent for LLM-based optimization modeling. Rather
than modifying skill construction, ArchOR starts from the
released OptSkills library, whose workflow-level skills con-
solidate successful and failed trajectories for optimization
archetypes. The proposed system changes how a query is
routed to those skills: CARL refines cached skill-vector
ordering, S3R imposes structural filtering, and baseline-
preserving arbitration retains the original route when struc-
tural coverage is uncertain. Two lightweight modules make
this archetype view operational. Centroid-Aware Represen-
tation Learning (CARL) transforms cached skill vectors with
archetype prototypes and a low-rank residual so that neigh-
boring skills are ordered by structural archetype rather than
surface wording. Signature-Guided Retrieval (S3R) attaches
an open-dimensional structural signature to every skill, with
attributes such as problem_class, var_pattern, and
constraint_family. At test time, a query signature
prioritizes compatible candidates by weighted overlap be-
fore LLM semantic re-ranking over a bounded candidate
set. Because neither signal is reliable on every cross-domain
query, ArchOR treats the inherited selector as a fallback and
overrides it only when inference-time evidence supports the
structural route.
Both components are needed because a fixed solver can
be effective for one family of optimization structures yet
arXiv:2610.41909v1  [cs.AI]  30 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
fail when the variable pattern or constraint family changes.
ArchOR therefore represents the problem structure, keeps a
portfolio of complementary workflow skills, and routes each
query to the most compatible workflow. CARL improves
the ordering of cached archetype representations, while S3R
provides a discrete guardrail against semantically plausible
but structurally wrong skills. Table 4 further validates the
representation-level improvement on the learned skill library.
Empirically, with the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash back-
bone (DeepSeek-AI 2026), ArchOR produces consistent
end-to-end accuracy improvements across five complemen-
tary benchmarks, while system-level and module ablations
separate retrieval quality, routing behavior, and arbitration
safety. Our contributions are threefold:
1. We identify retrieval as the limiting component of
archetype-centric skill libraries: raw cached skill vec-
tors can blur archetype boundaries, while semantics-only
skill cards can make structurally incompatible workflows
appear applicable.
2. We introduce two complementary modules that opera-
tionalize this view: one sharpens cached-vector neigh-
borhoods, and the other records auditable structural at-
tributes and uses their overlap to restrict the candidate set.
A baseline-preserving arbitration rule prevents incom-
plete signature coverage from discarding reliable baseline
skills.
3. We evaluate ArchOR across five benchmarks with the
same backbone and released skill library; system-level
ablations, module ablations, and leave-one-out retrieval
diagnostics show when structural routing helps and when
it must fall back to the baseline.
2
Related Work
2.1
Optimization Modeling with LLMs
Post-Training Methods.
A first line of work embeds opti-
mization competence directly into the model weights. Recent
representatives cover supervised fine-tuning (ORLM (Huang
et al. 2025a), OptMATH (Lu et al. 2025), AutoOR (Motwani
et al. 2026)), preference optimization (LLMOPT (Jiang et al.
2025a)), and reinforcement learning with solver-based re-
ward (SIRL (Chen et al. 2025), OR-R1 (Ding et al. 2026)).
Solver feedback gives these models a stronger training sig-
nal than ordinary instruction tuning, especially when the
objective value can be checked exactly. The cost is speci-
ficity: competence is tied to model parameters, updating it
requires additional training, and a deployed system cannot
easily inspect which learned procedure is being reused for a
new query. ArchOR instead keeps the backbone frozen and
places reusable procedures in an auditable skill library, so a
routing decision can be explained by cached-vector similar-
ity, signature overlap, and arbitration status.
These two families also imply different update cycles. A
fine-tuned checkpoint can enforce a consistent modeling style
and amortize competence into parameters, but correcting a
recurrent formulation error may require another training run
or a prompt workaround. A library can be versioned, in-
spected, and revised one workflow at a time. That trans-
parency shifts the burden from learning a procedure to de-
ciding when the procedure applies: an external skill is useful
only if the retriever preserves its boundary conditions and
the router does not override a safer known workflow.
Agent-Based Methods.
A second line keeps the base
model frozen and instead composes a multi-stage LLM
pipeline in which formulation, coding, execution, and re-
pair are handled by distinct agents. Chain-of-Experts (Xiao
et al. 2024) and OptiMUS (AhmadiTeshnizi, Gao, and Udell
2024) route sub-tasks through role-specialized experts glued
together by a conductor. ORMind (Wang et al. 2025) and
ORThought (Yang et al. 2025b) layer cognitive-style heuris-
tics on top of the pipeline so that business intent is progres-
sively refined into a mathematical formulation and executable
solver code. These systems improve error recovery and task
decomposition, but their reusable knowledge is usually en-
coded as prompts, agent roles, or execution habits rather
than as an explicitly indexed optimization workflow. Con-
sequently, two problems with the same variable pattern may
still be solved from scratch unless the pipeline itself main-
tains an external memory. ArchOR is complementary to
this direction: it supplies a structure-aware retrieval layer
that can decide when an existing workflow is applicable and
when the original selector should remain authoritative.
Experience-Enhanced Methods.
The design question
here is not merely whether experience should be reused,
but which artifact is indexed and what boundary controls
reuse.
Constraint-centered systems such as DRoC (Jiang
et al. 2025b) and ConstraintLLM (Shi et al. 2025) are effec-
tive when the bottleneck is translating stated requirements
into formal atoms, but isolated constraints do not specify the
order of modeling decisions or the checking steps required
after a solver returns. Exemplar-based systems such as MIR-
ROR (Shi et al. 2026) and LEAN-LLM-OPT (Liang et al.
2026) provide fuller scaffolds, yet a retrieved instance can
also import incidental quantities, objective conventions, or
domain assumptions. AlphaOPT (Kong et al. 2025) makes
those boundaries more explicit by refining insights from
failed attempts, although a lesson must still be matched at
the right level of generality. OptSkills (Yang et al. 2026a)
occupies an informative middle point: its reusable artifact
is an end-to-end workflow, while archetype clustering re-
duces dependence on narrative details during library con-
struction.
ArchOR starts after that construction step.
It
does not change how workflows are formed; instead, it deter-
mines whether a stored workflow is admissible for the current
query and whether it is safe to supersede the inherited base-
line route.
A closely related concurrent system, OptiSkill (Zhao et al.
2026), also builds a reusable optimization-specific skill bank,
organizing solver-verified experience into global strategies
and step-level error-prevention rules and evolving the bank
with validated test-time experience. Its emphasis is library
construction and evolution. ArchOR instead keeps the re-
leased OptSkills library frozen and studies the downstream
access decision: candidate admissibility, ordering, and over-
ride safety.


--- Page 3 ---
2.2
From Skill Acquisition to Skill Access
Research on agent skills can be viewed around a lifecy-
cle: XSkill (Jiang et al. 2026) asks what part of an execu-
tion trace should be abstracted into transferable procedure;
EvoSkill (Alzubi et al. 2026), Memento-Skills (Zhou et al.
2026), and AutoSkill (Yang et al. 2026b) study how a cat-
alog is discovered, routed to, and revised; Trace2Skill (Ni
et al. 2026) consolidates local trajectory lessons; and Mem-
Skill (Zhang et al. 2026) turns memory management itself
into a learned competence. SkillRet (Kang, Cho, and Kim
2026) further shows that selecting one skill from a large
library is itself a retrieval problem rather than an inciden-
tal prompt detail. This line shows that reusable knowledge
must be neither an unstructured trace nor an overly broad
prompt. It also makes clear that skill content and skill access
are separate problems: a well-formed catalog can still fail if
incompatible entries dominate the candidate list.
Optimization sharpens the access problem because com-
patibility is typed rather than merely topical. A candidate
must agree on decision roles, conservation and capacity re-
lations, objective orientation, integrality, and the assump-
tions expected by its solver backend. Two workflows can
share a transportation vocabulary while imposing different
directed-arc or shipment semantics; both may execute, but
only one represents the stated decision problem.
Multi-
signal structural-semantic consistency has also been used
to select generated MILP programs without solving every
candidate (Zeng et al. 2026); ArchOR addresses the com-
plementary earlier decision of retrieving an applicable work-
flow from a reusable skill library and deciding whether it
may override a stable baseline.
This separation suggests three operational requirements
for an access layer. The first is recall: plausible archetypes
must remain visible after caching, filtering, and re-ranking.
The second is typed admissibility: topical similarity can-
not authorize a workflow whose decision roles or solver
assumptions conflict with the query. The third is override
safety: a new route should replace a stable baseline only
when inference-time evidence indicates that it is executable
and structurally credible. Treating these requirements sep-
arately avoids collapsing retrieval quality into end-to-end
correctness, since a semantically near workflow can execute
successfully yet encode the wrong decision semantics. The
three components of ArchOR follow this decomposition:
CARL improves candidate ordering, S3R supplies explicit
compatibility evidence, and arbitration decides whether that
evidence is strong enough to supersede the inherited route.
ArchOR therefore contributes an access layer for a stable
optimization-skill library. CARL improves the geometry of
cached candidates, S3R supplies explicit compatibility at-
tributes, and arbitration controls when the resulting route
may supersede the baseline.
This separation is diagnos-
tic as well as empirical: signature overlap, candidate rank,
the chosen route, and solver validity distinguish omitted in-
gredients, over-broad aliases, ranking failures, and unsafe
overrides. It also explains why nearest-neighbor gains need
not imply end-to-end gains—an executable model with the
wrong semantics can still return a finite objective.
3
Methodology
ArchOR inherits the OptSkills (Yang et al. 2026a) skill
library, structural extractor, solver execution loop, and ver-
ification rule unchanged. Figure 1 summarizes the result-
ing inference pipeline. In the inherited interface, extracted
optimization ingredients and a scenario-neutral rewrite are
embedded and fused, while an LLM selector compares the
query with natural-language skill metadata over the library.
We keep this semantics-only route as the fallback baseline,
but focus on the missing retrieval decision: which skills are
structurally admissible, how those candidates should be or-
dered, and when the resulting structural route is allowed to
override the original selector. The proposed components are
therefore CARL, S3R, and baseline-preserving arbitration.
3.1
Centroid-Aware Representation Learning
CARL is implemented as a lightweight cached-vector pro-
totype residual. Each skill text is represented by a normal-
ized inverse-document-frequency vector zs. Skills carry an
archetype label when the label is available; unlabeled skills
are assigned to the nearest archetype center, and the centers
are recomputed after this deterministic assignment. Let aℓ
denote the center of archetype ℓ, let g(z) = arg maxℓz⊤aℓ,
and let Pr contain the top r right singular vectors of the
centered archetype centers. CARL maps
CARL(z) = Norm
␀z + λPrP ⊤
r
␀ag(z) −z

,
(1)
where λ = 0.35 and r = 16 in the reported setting. A query
is vectorized with the same vocabulary and IDF statistics,
transformed by Equation (1), and compared with transformed
skill vectors by cosine similarity. This realization requires
no GPU, no additional LLM call, and no gradient training;
it is a compact approximation of the archetype-aware repre-
sentation used to order candidate skills.
The construction has three steps. First, labeled skills are
grouped by archetype and each group is summarized by its
normalized centroid. Second, an unlabeled skill is attached
to the nearest centroid, after which the centroids are recom-
puted; this gives every library entry a prototype even when
the released metadata are incomplete. Third, the centered
prototype matrix is decomposed and only its top-r direc-
tions are used to move a cached vector toward its assigned
archetype.
The additive form is intentional: the original
token distribution remains available, while the correction
sharpens the directions along which archetypes differ. Con-
sequently, CARL changes only the candidate ordering and
does not alter a skill’s workflow, pitfalls, or applicability
boundary.
The transformation moves a query toward the nearest
cached archetype while constraining the correction to a low-
rank subspace.
The leave-one-out diagnostic in Table 4
shows that it increases Hit@1 from 0.607 to 0.804.
The
diagnostic also motivates the final arbitration rule: better
neighborhood ranking alone does not guarantee better end-
to-end solving accuracy when a query falls outside the cov-
erage of the current signature taxonomy.
The implementation applies the same transformation to
both sides of retrieval. Skill vectors are transformed once


--- Page 4 ---
Figure 1: Overview of ArchOR. Starting from the OptSkills skill library, CARL orders cached skill representations by
archetype similarity. Each skill and query also receives an open-dimensional structural signature. S3R first filters skills by
signature overlap and then invokes LLM semantic re-ranking only on the remaining candidates. Baseline-preserving arbitration
decides whether to use the structural route or preserve the original OptSkills route.
when the library is loaded; a query is first represented in
the shared vocabulary, assigned to its nearest prototype, pro-
jected onto the residual subspace, and normalized. Retrieval
then uses cosine similarity in this transformed space. This
symmetric treatment avoids the mismatch of comparing a
raw query with prototype-shifted skills. Since the library is
frozen, the repeated cost is only prototype lookup, a rank-r
projection, and similarity scoring; no encoder fine-tuning or
gradient update is introduced. The residual also gives a con-
trollable bias–variance trade-off: λ = 0 recovers the cached
representation, larger values impose stronger archetype ge-
ometry, and the low-rank basis prevents every token differ-
ence from being interpreted as an archetype boundary.
3.2
Open-Dimensional Skill Signatures
Natural-language skill cards are expressive but not directly
comparable. ArchOR therefore attaches a signature to each
skill. Given a cluster-level skill sC and its source trajectory
analyses, a Signature Extractor Σ emits
σs = Σ(sC, {qi | i ∈C}),
σs = {(k1, V1), . . . , (kL, VL)},
(2)
where each pair contains an attribute name and a set of
canonical tokens.
Examples include problem_class,
var_pattern,
constraint_family,
objective_form, and solver_backend. Canonical
aliases map surface terms such as “unit commitment” and
“binary run decision” to stable structural tokens.
The
schema is deliberately open-dimensional: attributes absent
for a skill may be omitted rather than forced into a fixed
taxonomy.
The same canonicalizer maps extracted query ingredients
and the scenario-neutral rewrite to σx. Signature construc-
tion reuses the structural-extraction call already performed
by the agent, so S3R does not require a separate retrieval
model. Unlike embedding similarity, signatures expose why
two items match, making the hard-filter stage deterministic
and auditable.
The signature layer is deliberately finer than a problem-
class label.
Two mixed-integer problems can differ in
whether binaries represent on/off capacity, assignment, rout-
ing arcs, or piecewise activation; two apparently similar flow
problems can differ in directed-arc semantics, source/sink
balance, or shipment integrality.
Therefore, a signature
records multiple attribute-value sets rather than a single class.
Missing attributes are omitted instead of being assigned a
meaningless default value, which keeps the schema extensi-
ble when the library encounters a new side condition.
Canonicalization is intended to preserve modeling seman-
tics rather than instance details. Numerical demands, costs,
and fleet sizes are not copied into the signature because they
change across queries in the same archetype; instead, the sig-
nature records the decision role, constraint family, objective
form, and solver assumption that determine whether a work-
flow is applicable. Synonyms are merged only when they
imply the same modeling structure. For example, startup
equipment, fixed opening cost, and binary run decision can
share a fixed-charge token, whereas a routing arc and an as-
signment binary remain distinct because they induce different
constraint matrices. This separation makes signature errors
easier to audit: a failed retrieval can be traced to a missing
attribute, an overly broad alias, or a wrongly canonicalized
token.


--- Page 5 ---
3.3
Signature-Guided Retrieval
At test time the library M∗is frozen. For every skill s ∈M∗,
S3R computes a weighted Jaccard affinity over attributes
present in both signatures:
J(σx, σs) =
X
k∈σx∩σs
ωk · |V x
k ∩V s
k |
|V x
k ∪V s
k |,
(3)
with ωk = 1/|σx ∩σs| by default. Attributes present in only
one signature contribute zero, and J = 0 when no attribute is
shared. Skills with positive overlap are ranked first; if fewer
than K skills have positive overlap, the remaining slots are
filled by library order so that structural sparsity does not
starve the selector. The resulting top-K set is denoted by
CK. We use K = 8.
CARL then orders the candidates in CK, and the LLM
performs semantic re-ranking only over this ordered subset.
Thus, semantics remains useful for final workflow choice,
but the selector cannot freely promote an arbitrary card from
the 46-skill catalog. When positive-overlap skills number
fewer than K, deterministic fallback entries preserve recall;
these entries remain subject to the later arbitration check.
This stage combines a discrete prioritization signal with a
continuous ordering signal. Positive Jaccard overlap places
a skill in the structural tier before fallback entries are consid-
ered. CARL then determines the order in which candidates
are presented, which matters because the selector receives
only a short list and is sensitive to neighborhood quality.
Candidate construction is organized as two explicit tiers.
Skills with positive weighted overlap form the structural tier,
with affinity determining tier membership; fallback entries
are used only when this tier has fewer than K members.
Within the final candidate set, CARL supplies the contin-
uous presentation order and the LLM selector supplies the
final workflow choice. The affinity, shared attributes, se-
lected skill, and candidate rank are logged for each query,
so a failure can be distinguished from selector misunder-
standing, structural over-filtering, or an incorrect workflow
execution. This audit trail is a direct consequence of rep-
resenting compatibility as attributes rather than only as an
embedding score.
3.4
Baseline-Preserving Integration
Structural filtering is useful only when its signature cover-
age matches the query. To prevent an incomplete signature
taxonomy from discarding a reliable baseline skill, ArchOR
preserves the original OptSkills route and arbitrates be-
tween the two routes using only inference-time information.
Let b denote the baseline route and a the CARL+S3R
route. Let cb and ca be their selector confidences, let ra
be the rank of the selected structural skill in CK, and let
V (ya) indicate that route a returns a nonempty, finite solver
prediction. ArchOR uses the structural route when
V (ya) ∧(cb ≤0.62 ∨ca > cb ∨ra ≥7) .
(4)
Otherwise it returns the baseline route. The rule does not use
the ground-truth answer, the objective gap, or any evaluation
label. It accepts the structural route when the baseline se-
lector is uncertain, when the structural selector is more con-
fident, or when the selected skill appears late in the filtered
candidate list. In the five-benchmark evaluation, this rule
routes 374 of 1,100 queries through the structural branch and
preserves the baseline branch for the remaining 726 queries.
Each condition addresses a different observed failure
mode.
The low-confidence threshold handles queries for
which the baseline selector has already identified several
plausible but indistinguishable skills. The confidence-gain
condition allows structural evidence to break a semantic tie.
The late-rank condition is coverage-oriented: if the selected
structural skill appears near the boundary of CK, it may
encode a specialized assumption that the natural-language
card did not reveal. Requiring V (ya) excludes empty, non-
finite, or execution-failed structural predictions before they
can replace a usable baseline answer.
In practice, integration is a routing procedure rather than
a new solver.
The system first records the baseline skill
and confidence, extracts the query signature, constructs CK,
obtains the structural selection and its solver output, and
then applies Equation (4). If arbitration rejects the structural
route, the original OptSkills answer is returned unchanged.
Thus, S3R can reduce the selector’s search space without
being allowed to delete the baseline path, and CARL can im-
prove candidate ordering without being treated as evidence of
correctness by itself. This separation is what makes the final
system robust to incomplete signatures while still allowing
structural evidence to correct semantic mistakes.
Library refinement and expansion operators are inherited
unchanged from OptSkills. In the main evaluation the re-
leased learned library is frozen, so the comparison isolates
retrieval and arbitration rather than additional library growth.
4
Experiments
Setup.
The
controlled
comparison
uses
the
same
self-hosted DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone (DeepSeek-AI
2026). We use the official OptSkills repository, its released
learned skill library, and the official five evaluation sets:
OptiBench (Yang et al. 2025c) (605 queries), OptMATH-
Bench (Lu et al. 2025) (166), Mamo.C (Huang et al. 2025b)
(211), IndustryOR (Huang et al. 2025a) (100), and Com-
plexOR (Xiao et al. 2024) (18), for 1,100 queries in total.
The baseline is the unmodified OptSkills semantic selector.
ArchOR adds the CARL and S3R routes described in Sec-
tion 3. For context, Table 1 also retains the external-baseline
results reported by OptSkills (Yang et al. 2026a) under its
original evaluation protocol.
Protocol.
The five suites are deliberately complementary.
OptiBench and Mamo.C stress natural-language modeling
and LP/MILP structures, OptMATH contains longer and
more diverse solver-verified formulations, IndustryOR intro-
duces practical business scenarios, and ComplexOR requires
implicit constraints and multi-step combinatorial reasoning.
Reporting both averages therefore avoids interpreting a gain
on short textbook-style prompts as general optimization com-
petence. The controlled systems use temperature 0, request
seed 42, a maximum generation length of 8,192 tokens, eight
evaluation workers, a 120-second solver timeout, and at most
12 agent turns. Each controlled system is evaluated once per
query. The selector returns three solver candidates. S3R uses


--- Page 6 ---
K = 8; CARL uses strength 0.35 and residual rank 16. A
query is correct only when the executed solver returns a finite
objective value equal to the rounded ground truth, or when
rounded values are unavailable and the absolute gap is at
most 0.005. We report Macro-Avg. over the five benchmark
accuracies and Micro-Avg. over all 1,100 queries. External
rows follow the evaluation protocol used in the OptSkills
report and are not re-run here.
The arbitration constants
are fixed globally for all reported queries: cb ≤0.62 and
ra ≥7. They are not adapted per query or per benchmark;
independent calibration of these thresholds remains future
work.
The experiments evaluate same-backbone end-to-end im-
provement over OptSkills, the individual and combined
effects of CARL and S3R, whether CARL improves retrieval
quality independently of final solver success, and where
baseline-preserving arbitration helps or fails.
4.1
End-to-End Results
Same-backbone comparison.
Table 1 shows that Ar-
chOR improves Macro-Avg. by 2.68 pp and Micro-Avg. by
1.64 pp over the controlled OptSkills baseline. The gain
corresponds to 18 additional correct answers (697 →715);
an exact McNemar test on the 23 improved and 5 degraded
paired outcomes gives p = 0.0009. Improvements occur on
all five benchmarks, with the largest absolute gains on Com-
plexOR (5.55 pp), OptMATH (4.22 pp), and IndustryOR
(2.00 pp). ArchOR also has the highest averaged accura-
cies in the combined table, although the causal comparison
is restricted to the controlled systems because the external
rows follow their original settings. The smaller OptiBench
and Mamo.C gains reflect the mixed coverage of the current
structural signatures: the modules help on many queries but
can still discard a reliable baseline skill when the signature
schema is incomplete.
Context among external systems.
Among the retained
OptSkills-reported results, Trace2Skill is the strongest ex-
ternal baseline, with 63.46% Micro-Avg. and 56.97% Macro-
Avg. ArchOR is 1.54 pp higher in Micro-Avg. and 3.64 pp
higher in Macro-Avg., but we treat this as contextual rather
than a same-setting claim because the external systems use
different backbones and protocols. The benchmark profile
is nevertheless informative. ArchOR has the highest Opt-
MATH result (69.88%) and ties for the best IndustryOR
result (35.00%), where reusable solver workflows and ex-
plicit variable/constraint structure are especially valuable. It
reaches 72.22% on ComplexOR, matching the best listed re-
sult, while Trace2Skill remains stronger on OptiBench and
AlphaOPT remains slightly stronger on Mamo.C. This pat-
tern suggests that structural retrieval is most useful when
the narrative is difficult but the underlying optimization
archetype can still be recovered reliably.
4.2
Routing and Representation Ablations
Why direct structural routing is insufficient.
Table 2
shows that replacing the baseline selector on every query
is harmful: direct CARL+S3R obtains 61.45% Micro-Avg.,
1.91 pp below OptSkills. Relative to the baseline, direct
routing turns 39 wrong answers into correct answers but
also turns 60 correct answers into wrong answers (exact Mc-
Nemar p = 0.044). The cause is coverage: the signature
taxonomy does not yet cover every cross-domain narrative,
so the top-8 structural filter can remove a baseline skill that
would have succeeded. Baseline-preserving arbitration re-
moves most of this regression: relative to OptSkills, Ar-
chOR turns 23 wrong answers into correct answers and only
5 correct answers into wrong answers.
The OptMATH ablation in Table 3 shows that neither
module is uniformly beneficial when used as a mandatory
replacement. CARL-only and S3R-only each lose 4.21 pp
relative to the baseline, while their direct combination loses
3.01 pp. In contrast, the integrated system gains 4.22 pp.
This distinction is the main empirical motivation for arbitra-
tion: CARL improves neighborhood ranking, S3R reduces
the selector input, but neither signal alone is reliable enough
to override the baseline on every query.
Direct routing improves ComplexOR and IndustryOR
when signatures match, but loses 1.90–3.01 pp on the other
three suites when extraction is incomplete. Arbitration re-
tains the two gains while recovering those losses: structural
retrieval is used as selective evidence, not as a universal
replacement.
Retrieval diagnostic.
Table 4 evaluates cached skill rep-
resentations with a leave-one-out protocol in which a query
is correct when a skill of the same problem class appears
among its neighbors. CARL increases Hit@1 from 0.607
to 0.804, Hit@3 from 0.732 to 0.893, Hit@5 from 0.821 to
0.893, and MRR from 0.682 to 0.839. Thus, the represen-
tation change is effective at the retrieval level even though
mandatory structural routing does not improve end-to-end
accuracy.
The module ablation also separates representation quality
from decision policy.
A better nearest-neighbor ordering
does not determine whether the baseline route should be
abandoned, and a smaller candidate set is helpful only if the
retained skills cover the binding structure of the query. The
large MRR gain in Table 4 is nevertheless relevant because
the LLM selector sees only a short candidate list: moving
the correct archetype toward the top can affect selection even
when the correct skill already appears among five neighbors.
Routing analysis.
The final system uses the structural
branch on 374 queries and preserves the baseline branch
on 726 queries. The most useful cases are those in which
the baseline selector has low confidence, the structural se-
lector has higher confidence, or a structurally plausible skill
appears late in the filtered candidate list. Failures remain in
three forms: the extractor can omit a binding ingredient, the
signature can assign a coarse but incomplete problem class,
and two routes can select different skills whose workflows
are both syntactically valid but encode different assumptions.
These failures motivate a larger independently calibrated sig-
nature taxonomy and a conditional online implementation
that executes the second route only when the two selectors
disagree.

Case study.
Full problem statements and route details are
in Appendix A. S1 corrects a low-confidence knapsack mis-
assignment with a fixed-charge workflow. S2 shows that a
late-rank structural skill can repair an overconfident wrong
baseline. F1 is the mirror image: the same late-rank rule
overrides a correct transportation answer with an incompati-
ble flow workflow. Thus, arbitration helps when the baseline
archetype is wrong, but is risky when coarse signatures con-
flate different flow assumptions.
5
Conclusion
ArchOR builds on OptSkills and improves its retrieval
space with CARL and S3R. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-
Flash backbone and released skill library, the integrated sys-

cb is baseline
confidence and ra is the rank in CK.
Case
Benchmark / trigger
Baseline →structural
S1
OptiBench #579; cb=.55, ra=1
knapsack 360,000 →fixed-charge 3,600 ✓
S2

Mamo.C #133; cb=.95, ra=8
transportation 1,490 →flow 16,381 ×
tem obtains a 1.64 pp Micro-Avg. gain over OptSkills across
five benchmarks, while the signature gate reduces the maxi-
mum selector input from 46 skills to 8. Directly replacing the
selector on every query is harmful, but baseline-preserving
arbitration preserves most baseline successes and captures
additional structural successes. Looking forward, expanding
the signature taxonomy on independent calibration data, im-
plementing a conditional online version that executes the sec-
ond route after selector disagreement, and adding symbolic
verification of extracted structures are natural next steps.

A
Qualitative Case Studies
This appendix expands the three arbitration cases summa-
rized in Table 5. For each case we report the (condensed)
problem statement, the baseline and structural skill choices
with their selector confidences, the rank ra of the structural
skill in the S3R-filtered list, and the solver-verified objective
values against the ground truth.
Only the confidence values used by the reported routing
decisions are included.
A.1
Success S1: Signature Recovers a
Fixed-Charge Pricing Archetype
Benchmark. OptiBench, query #579.
Problem. Choose a selling price in increments of $0.10.
At a price of $1.50 demand is 5,000 units, and every $0.10
reduction adds 1,000 units. Production has a $2,000 start-up
cost and a $0.50 per-unit cost. Maximize total profit.
Routing.
The
baseline
selector
chooses
integer_linear_programming_
with_multiple_knapsack_constraints
with
confidence cb = 0.55.
Its solver path reports 360,000,
while the ground-truth optimum is 3,600—a 100× over-
estimate caused by modeling the problem as a generic
knapsack-style allocation.
The extracted signature in-
stead contains problem_class={fixed_charge},
variables
{price_decision,
sales_quantity, nonnegative_integer},
and
constraints
{price_multiple,
demand_price_relationship}.
S3R
places
fixed_charge_production_planning
at
rank
ra = 1, and its workflow returns exactly 3,600.
Decision.
Arbitration activates the structural route be-
cause cb = 0.55 ≤0.62 and the structural confidence is
higher (ca = 0.72 > 0.55).
This case illustrates the in-
tended use of the low-confidence and confidence-gain trig-
gers: the narrative mentions no knapsack or capacity struc-
ture, and the signature correctly separates the fixed-charge
pricing archetype from generic integer allocation.
A.2
Success S2: Late-Rank Promotion Corrects
an Overconfident Baseline
Benchmark. IndustryOR, query #43.
Problem.
A
company
with
40
workers
(20
units/worker/month) must meet six monthly demands
(700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800). Flexibility comes from over-
time (at most 6 units/worker/month at EUR 5/unit), inven-
tory (EUR 10/unit/month), and workforce changes (±5 per
month; hiring EUR 500, layoff EUR 700). Inventory starts
and must end empty. Meet all demands at minimum total
overtime, inventory, hiring, and layoff cost, and report the
relaxed-objective value.
Routing.
The
baseline
selector
chooses
multi_period_production_
inventory_planning
with
high
confidence
cb = 0.95, but its solver path returns −10,000 whereas
the correct relaxed objective is +10,000.
The struc-
tural signature captures the operative decision struc-
ture.
Its
variables
are
production_quantity,
inventory_level,
workforce_level,
overtime_production,
hiring_quantity,
and
layoff_quantity;
its
constraints
are
demand_satisfaction,
inventory_balance,
workforce_change_limit,
overtime_capacity_limit,
and
terminal_inventory.
The
selected
structural
skill,
generator_commitment_and_dispatch,
appears only at rank ra = 8; its workflow nevertheless
encodes the on/off capacity and dispatch structure that
matches overtime and workforce adjustment, and returns the
exact value 10,000.
Decision. The late-rank condition ra = 8 ≥7 activates
the structural route despite the high baseline confidence. This
case shows why confidence alone is an insufficient arbitration
signal: a selector can be certain about the wrong archetype,
and a structurally appropriate workflow can rank late when
the signature is only partially extracted.
A.3
Failure F1: The Same Late-Rank Trigger
Overrides a Correct Baseline
Benchmark. Mamo.C, query #133.
Problem.
Six
cities
hold
food
supplies
of
255, 250, 314, 8, 385, 440
tons
and
require
251, 200, 366, 114, 59, 287 tons.
Supplies may be re-
located along an asymmetric cost matrix.
Satisfy all
requirements at minimum transportation cost.
Routing.
The
baseline
selector
chooses
transportationproblemsolver
with
confidence
cb = 0.95 and returns the correct optimum 1,490.
The
signature is also structurally sensible: its problem classes
are resource_allocation and transportation;
its
variables
are
transportation_quantity,
flow_variable, and nonnegative_continuous;
and
its
constraints
are
flow_balance,
demand_satisfaction, and flow_conservation.
The
structural
route
selects
the
same-family
skill
transportation_flow_optimizer at rank ra = 8.
However, that workflow encodes different flow assumptions
and returns 16,381, an order of magnitude above the
optimum.
Decision. The same late-rank condition that rescued S2
activates here and replaces a correct answer with an incor-
rect one. The failure is not caused by a wrong archetype
label: both skills plausibly match the transportation signa-
ture. Instead, the taxonomy is too coarse to distinguish which
flow formulation each workflow implements (e.g., directed-
arc capacities, source/sink semantics, or integrality of ship-
ments). This motivates refining signature attributes below
the problem-class level and conditioning the late-rank trigger
on additional evidence of baseline fragility, such as solver-
path failure or selector disagreement.
